extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, judges, and parties litigating or evaluating design-patent validity
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and analytical framework for evaluating nonobviousness of U.S. design patent claims under 35 U.S.C. § 103, as articulated by the Federal Circuit en banc in LKQ v. GM. Focuses on how to apply Graham factors, analogous art, primary/secondary references, and secondary considerations in the design context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patents subject to § 103 nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patents must meet the nonobviousness requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 103; the provisions relating to utility patents apply to design patents unless otherwise provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the statutory language of § 103 to design claims, recognizing differences between utility and design patents (e.g., focus on overall appearance, visual impressions, artistry, and style rather than function or utility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Graham factors to design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness of a design patent claim should be determined based on factual criteria similar to those used for utility patents under Graham v. John Deere Co.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Graham framework as adapted to designs: (1) scope and content of the prior art (with analogous art limitation), (2) differences between the prior art and the claimed design, (3) the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art (ordinary designer), and (4) consideration of secondary considerations/indicia of (non)obviousness when presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and content of the prior art / analogous art requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: References qualify for an obviousness determination only when they are analogous to the claimed design; analogous art defines the knowledge base of the person of ordinary skill and guards against hindsight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat analogous art as a gateway: a reference must be in an art reasonably pertinent to the claimed design (typically same field of endeavor) or otherwise analogous. The analogous art test limits what may be considered in the obviousness inquiry and helps prevent reconstruction of the invention with hindsight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify a primary reference (closest / visually most similar prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: An obviousness analysis should begin with identification of a primary prior-art design, typically the prior art design most visually similar to the claimed design, but there is no rigid 'basically the same' threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The primary reference serves as the starting point for the obviousness inquiry; it need only be analogous and suitably similar to be a reasonable starting reference, not 'basically the same' in the rigid sense used by Rosen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate differences between the prior art and the claimed design (overall visual impression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the differences between the claimed design and the prior art in terms of the overall visual impression created by the design as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the claimed design and prior art holistically (overall visual impression) and identify the specific differences (e.g., shapes, lines, creases, terminus). Do not conflate this inquiry with anticipation; for design patents, the visual impression as a whole is central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of ordinary skill in the art (ordinary designer perspective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine what a person of ordinary skill in the relevant design field would know and would find predictable; this perspective frames the obviousness analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the ordinary designer's knowledge to assess scope of prior art, appropriate combinations, and motivations to modify a primary reference; analogous art is tied to this perspective because that person could reasonably be aware of analogous art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary references and modification: record-supported reason to modify primary reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary prior-art designs may be used to modify a primary reference when there is some record-supported reason that an ordinary designer would have modified the primary reference in light of the secondary reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than requiring the Durling 'so related' test, permit secondary references where the record shows a motivation or reason (e.g., customary practice, market design pressures, known combinations) that would lead an ordinary designer to apply features from the secondary to the primary reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject rigid 'basically the same' and 'so related' requirements (overrule Rosen-Durling)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rosen requirement that a primary reference be 'basically the same' and Durling's requirement that secondary references be 'so related' are improperly rigid and inconsistent with § 103 and KSR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a flexible, common-sense approach to motivation to combine; do not terminate the obviousness inquiry merely because no single prior-art design is 'basically the same' as the claimed design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use KSR-style flexible motivations to combine
rubrics_metrics.description: Motivation to combine prior art for obviousness may be shown by a variety of reasons beyond a formalistic teaching-suggestion-motivation (TSM) test, including market forces, design incentives, customary practice, or 'obvious to try' where there are finite predictable solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow factfinders to rely on common sense and ordinary-design practice (subject to evidentiary support) to find motivation to combine, while guarding against hindsight bias through analogous art and corroborating record evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against hindsight and improper combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinations assembled only with the benefit of hindsight or from non-analogous arts that reconstruct the claimed design are insufficient to prove obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that combining references is supported by analogous-art analysis and record evidence demonstrating that an ordinary designer would have reasonably made the combination without impermissible hindsight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation / Gorham ordinary observer test for design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: For anticipation and infringement questions, apply the Gorham ordinary-observer test: if in the eye of an ordinary observer giving such attention as a purchaser usually gives, two designs are substantially the same, infringement/anticipation is present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation requires that the prior design create 'substantially the same' overall visual impression (i.e., deceive an ordinary observer); this is a distinct inquiry from § 103 obviousness analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations (objective indicia) apply to design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: When presented, secondary considerations such as commercial success, industry praise, and copying may be used as indicia of nonobviousness for design patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider objective evidence of nonobviousness (commercial success, praise, copying); the opinion reaffirms existing precedent applying these to design patents but notes uncertainty about applicability of other factors (e.g., long-felt need) in the design context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid detailed verbal claim construction for design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: The process for claim construction in design patent cases should not require a detailed verbal description of the claimed design like in utility patents; designs are better represented pictorially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunals should adapt claim construction to a pictorial setting and avoid over-reliance on detailed verbal descriptions that could distort the ordinary-observer/visual-impression analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factfinder evidentiary role and remand procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the new framework, factfinders (e.g., the PTAB) must reassess nonobviousness by applying Graham factors, analogous art, and record-supported reasons for combining references; appellate courts may vacate and remand for this evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On remand, the trier of fact should identify a primary reference, evaluate analogous art, identify any record-supported motivations to modify or combine references, apply Graham factors (including secondary considerations), and make findings supported by substantial evidence while avoiding hindsight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between anticipation and obviousness inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not conflate the Gorham-based ordinary-observer anticipation test (substantially the same) with the § 103 obviousness inquiry (differences such that the design as a whole would have been obvious).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation ends the analysis if a design is substantially the same; obviousness may still be found by combining references under § 103 even when no single prior design is substantially the same, provided the combination is supported and not the result of hindsight.
